# Exact perturbation criterion at a sharp heavy endpoint

This file gives an unconditional reduction and a sharpness qualification.
It does not prove the proposed middle-fiber transfer in arbitrary d>=2.

## Setup

Let d>=1 and let A,K,B be d-dimensional convex bodies. Put

    a=vol_d(A), k=vol_d(K), b=vol_d(B),

and assume

    (A+B)/2 subset K,  a=k+b.                           (1)

Form C=conv( {-1}xA, {0}xK, {1}xB ). These are exactly its three
integer fibers; the middle-fiber assertion follows directly from (1).
Its mixed-integer measure mu has total mass 2a.

For a continuous body E, write

    beta(E)=max_{x in E} inf_{J containing x} vol_d(E intersect J),

where J ranges over closed d-dimensional halfspaces. Let

    gamma=gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d,
    D=max_{x in K} inf_{H containing (0,x)} mu(H).        (2)

The proposed transfer is D>=gamma a. It is a condition on the entire
middle fiber, not on any centroid segment.

## 1. Endpoint depths are exactly their ordinary continuous depths

For x in A, its mixed-integer depth at (-1,x), in unnormalized mass,
equals its ordinary unnormalized halfspace depth in A. Any ambient
containing halfspace cuts at least that mass from the A fiber. Conversely,
given a containing continuous halfspace on A, add a sufficiently large
negative coefficient of z+1 to its defining linear functional. This
preserves its cut on A and excludes the bounded K and B fibers. The
same argument with the opposite tilt works at B.

Consequently the maximum depths on the endpoint fibers are beta(A)
and beta(B). If A is a simplex, beta(A)=gamma a exactly. More generally,
the perturbation argument below only requires the sharpness assumption

    beta(A)=gamma a.                                   (3)

Without (3), a small shrink of A need not make its endpoint suboptimal:
beta(A)>gamma a can survive such a perturbation. This is why the
shape qualification is substantive.

## 2. Balance and BM make the other endpoint automatically harmless

Classical Brunn-Minkowski and arithmetic-geometric mean give

    k >= ((a^(1/d)+b^(1/d))/2)^d >=sqrt(ab).

Combining this with a=k+b yields

    k^2>=b(k+b),
    b/k<=(sqrt(5)-1)/2<2/3.                            (4)

In particular b<a/2 and 2b<a. Every ordinary continuous-body depth is
at most half its volume, by considering the two opposite halfspaces
through a point; their common hyperplane has zero volume. Thus

    beta(B)<=b/2<k/3<gamma k.                          (5)

For completeness gamma>1/3 follows from

    (1+1/d)^d <=sum_(j=0)^d 1/j! <3.

The last strict bound follows by bounding the factorial series tail
with a geometric series. Therefore B need not be a simplex for the
sharp-endpoint perturbation argument.

## 3. Attainment of the middle maximum

The maximum D in (2) is attained. The set K is compact. Depth for a
finite compactly supported measure is upper semicontinuous: if y_j
tends to y and H={ell>=t} contains y, the enlarged closed halfspace
H_epsilon={ell>=t-epsilon} contains y_j eventually. Hence

    limsup depth(y_j)<=mu(H_epsilon).

Let epsilon decrease to zero and use continuity from above, then take
the infimum over H. This argument retains every positive boundary-fiber
mass. Upper semicontinuity on K gives attainment.

Thus failure of transfer means the actual strict inequality

    D<gamma a,                                         (6)

not merely failure of a chosen candidate or an unattained supremum.

## 4. An explicit allowed shrink converts strict transfer failure to OC failure

Assume (3) and (6). Choose a mass decrement satisfying

    0<Delta<min{2b, 2(gamma a-D)/gamma}.                 (7)

The interval in (7) is nonempty. Choose any a_0 in A and let

    r=(1-Delta/a)^(1/d), A_r=a_0+r(A-a_0).

Since 2b<a, condition (7) gives 0<r<1. Convexity gives A_r subset A,
and vol(A_r)=a-Delta. Keeping K and B fixed preserves (1)'s midpoint
containment. Thus

    C_r=conv( {-1}xA_r, {0}xK, {1}xB )

is a convex body with exactly those three integer fibers. Its measure
mu_r is a submeasure of mu, with total mass

    M_r=2a-Delta,

and its required OC threshold is

    T_r=(gamma/2)M_r=gamma(a-Delta/2).                  (8)

Every point of the middle fiber is bad: mu_r<=mu implies its depth
is at most D, while (7) gives D<T_r.

Every point of the A_r endpoint is bad: homothety preserves normalized
ordinary depth, so its endpoint maximum is

    beta(A_r)=gamma(a-Delta)<T_r.

Every point of the B endpoint is also bad. By Delta<2b,

    T_r>gamma(a-b)=gamma k>beta(B),

using (5). Hence all mixed-integer points of C_r violate the OC bound.

All three perturbed fibers are in fact nonheavy: A_r has volume below
M_r/2 because Delta>0; K has volume below M_r/2 because Delta<2b;
and B is smaller than K by (4). No limiting or continuity theorem is
needed for the mass comparison: only the exact inclusion A_r subset A.

If a rational shrink is required for rational polytopes, choose rational
r<1 sufficiently close to one so that Delta=a(1-r^d) satisfies (7).
This follows directly from continuity of that polynomial and preserves
the rational geometry.

## Consequence and logical scope

Under the sharp-endpoint assumption (3), any certified strict failure
of middle transfer at balance yields an explicit nearby three-fiber
counterexample to OC. The other endpoint can be an arbitrary convex
body; its depth is controlled by (4)-(5).

This is an unconditional implication, not a proof that transfer holds.
Invoking OC for the perturbed family to deduce transfer would be circular
in the present task. It also explains why falsifying transfer in the
sharp-simplex case is substantially stronger than the previous centroid
convex-hull obstruction: that obstruction only excludes a line segment
inside K, whereas (6) must bound every point of K.

For the previously constructed triangular family, the balanced instance
is eta=0 in `candidate 84ed2ea21a94e03a`. Its centroid-hull
segment is still covered by the two bad caps, but that coverage says
nothing about the rest of K. The present reduction cannot be triggered
by that segment certificate.

## 5. Complete interval case, with an exact stronger value

When d=1, the transfer holds directly. Translate the continuous
coordinate by an affine function of z so that the centers of A and B
become zero. This shear preserves Z x R, all fiber lengths, and the
full halfspace family. Write

    A=[-a/2,a/2], B=[-b/2,b/2],
    K=[h-k/2,h+k/2].

Midpoint containment says K contains [-(a+b)/4,(a+b)/4]. Since
k=a-b, this implies

    |h|<=(a-3b)/4<=(a-b)/4.

Therefore 2h-B subset A: the reflected interval has center 2h and
radius b/2, both of which fit in the interval of radius a/2. The
mixed subset consisting of the whole B fiber at z=1 and its reflection
inside A at z=-1 is centrally symmetric about (0,h), with mass 2b.
Every closed halfspace through (0,h) captures at least b from it.
The middle interval contributes at least k/2 because h is its center.
Thus

    depth_mu(0,h)>=k/2+b=(a+b)/2>a/2=gamma_1 a.

This lower bound is also exact at that point: choose either half of K
through h and add a sufficiently large positive integer-coordinate
normal to include all of B and exclude all of A. Its mass is k/2+b.
This proves the interval transfer without invoking OC for a perturbed
family or relying on an unproved multivariate target law.

## 6. The full-reflected-B mechanism has an exact planar obstruction

The reflection containment used in Section 5 cannot be assumed in
higher dimension, even when both endpoints are simplices and balance
holds exactly. In R^2 let

    A=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)},
    B=conv{(0,0),(7/5,0),(0,1/100)},
    K=conv{(0,0),(6/5,0),(7/10,1/2),(0,193/350)}.

Their areas are

    a=1/2, b=7/1000, k=493/1000,

so a=k+b. The endpoint Minkowski average is the quadrilateral

    (A+B)/2=conv{(0,0),(6/5,0),(7/10,1/2),(0,101/200)}.

The first three vertices are shared with K and 101/200<193/350, so
the fourth lies on the vertical edge of K. This proves the required
midpoint containment exactly. The quadrilaterals are convex in the
displayed cyclic order; their areas also follow immediately from
the shoelace formula.

For every point x in R^2, the reflected set 2x-B has horizontal width
7/5, whereas A has horizontal width one. Therefore

    {x:2x-B subset A}=empty.

So a proof demanding a full symmetric copy of B inside A, at some
middle center, cannot treat all balanced sharp-endpoint instances.
This is an obstruction to that mechanism only, not to the transfer
claim itself. Partial reflected overlap or a different transport
would require a separate quantitative estimate.
